claim: Plasmodium vivax is the second most prevalent malarial pathogen.
source: Plasmodium vivax is the second most prevalent malarial pathogen, with a wider geographical distribution than P. falciparum, suggested to be a risk of malaria infection for 2.5 billion people (Howes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howes et al., 2016

claim: P. vivax has a wider geographical distribution than P. falciparum.
source: Plasmodium vivax is the second most prevalent malarial pathogen, with a wider geographical distribution than P. falciparum, suggested to be a risk of malaria infection for 2.5 billion people (Howes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howes et al., 2016

claim: P. vivax poses a risk of malaria infection for 2.5 billion people.
source: Plasmodium vivax is the second most prevalent malarial pathogen, with a wider geographical distribution than P. falciparum, suggested to be a risk of malaria infection for 2.5 billion people (Howes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howes et al., 2016

claim: An estimated 8.5 million new clinical cases of P. vivax were reported in 2016 globally.
source: According to the WHO report (2017), an estimated 8.5 million new clinical cases of P. vivax was reported in 2016 globally.
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO report 2017

claim: P. vivax research is restricted to few laboratories.
source: Despite its high prevalence in many malaria endemic countries, P. vivax research is restricted to few laboratories and limited progress has been made (Armistead and Adams, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Armistead and Adams, 2018

claim: Limited progress has been made in P. vivax research.
source: Despite its high prevalence in many malaria endemic countries, P. vivax research is restricted to few laboratories and limited progress has been made (Armistead and Adams, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Armistead and Adams, 2018

claim: The FDA recently approved tafenoquine as a radical cure therapy and prophylactic for P. vivax malaria infection.
source: Notwithstanding, the FDA recently approved tafenoquine as a radical cure therapy and prophylactic for P. vivax malaria infection (Frampton, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frampton, 2018

claim: Tafenoquine is administered as a single dose regimen.
source: This is a significant advance as tafenoquine is administered as a single dose regimen, which is a very important improvement for patient compliance when compared to the lengthy 14-day drug regimen of its closely related predecessor primaquine.
evidence: Stated directly in the text

claim: Primaquine requires a 14-day drug regimen.
source: This is a significant advance as tafenoquine is administered as a single dose regimen, which is a very important improvement for patient compliance when compared to the lengthy 14-day drug regimen of its closely related predecessor primaquine.
evidence: Stated directly in the text

claim: Tafenoquine is only approved for patients over the age of 16.
source: However, tafenoquine is only approved for patients over the age of 16 and, like primaquine, it cannot be administered to patients who have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, a common genetic disorder in malaria endemic countries, due to serious adverse side-effects and life-threatening drug-induced hemolysis (Wells et al., 2010; Mazier et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wells et al., 2010 and Mazier et al., 2009

claim: Tafenoquine cannot be administered to patients who have G6PD deficiency.
source: However, tafenoquine is only approved for patients over the age of 16 and, like primaquine, it cannot be administered to patients who have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, a common genetic disorder in malaria endemic countries, due to serious adverse side-effects and life-threatening drug-induced hemolysis (Wells et al., 2010; Mazier et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wells et al., 2010 and Mazier et al., 2009

claim: G6PD deficiency is a common genetic disorder in malaria endemic countries.
source: However, tafenoquine is only approved for patients over the age of 16 and, like primaquine, it cannot be administered to patients who have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, a common genetic disorder in malaria endemic countries, due to serious adverse side-effects and life-threatening drug-induced hemolysis (Wells et al., 2010; Mazier et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wells et al., 2010 and Mazier et al., 2009

claim: Tafenoquine and primaquine cause serious adverse side-effects and life-threatening drug-induced hemolysis in G6PD deficient patients.
source: However, tafenoquine is only approved for patients over the age of 16 and, like primaquine, it cannot be administered to patients who have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, a common genetic disorder in malaria endemic countries, due to serious adverse side-effects and life-threatening drug-induced hemolysis (Wells et al., 2010; Mazier et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wells et al., 2010 and Mazier et al., 2009

claim: New drugs are critically needed to enable malaria elimination.
source: Therefore, new drugs are critically needed to enable malaria elimination.
evidence: Logical inference from the limitations of current drugs

claim: Malaria transmission begins when uni-nucleated sporozoites are transmitted by mosquito bite.
source: Malaria transmission begins when uni-nucleated sporozoites are transmitted by mosquito bite, reach the liver and invade hepatocytes within which they transform into multi-nucleated hepatic schizonts.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about malaria transmission

claim: Sporozoites reach the liver and invade hepatocytes.
source: Malaria transmission begins when uni-nucleated sporozoites are transmitted by mosquito bite, reach the liver and invade hepatocytes within which they transform into multi-nucleated hepatic schizonts.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about malaria transmission

claim: Sporozoites transform into multi-nucleated hepatic schizonts within hepatocytes.
source: Malaria transmission begins when uni-nucleated sporozoites are transmitted by mosquito bite, reach the liver and invade hepatocytes within which they transform into multi-nucleated hepatic schizonts.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about malaria transmission

claim: Mature schizonts release merozoites that infect red blood cells.
source: Mature schizonts release merozoites that infect red blood cells (RBCs) and lead to the onset of clinical symptoms associated with malaria.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about malaria transmission

claim: Merozoite infection of RBCs leads to the onset of clinical symptoms associated with malaria.
source: Mature schizonts release merozoites that infect red blood cells (RBCs) and lead to the onset of clinical symptoms associated with malaria.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about malaria transmission

claim: Sporozoites of P. vivax, P. ovale and P. cynomolgi can generate latent forms known as hypnozoites.
source: Remarkably, sporozoites of P. vivax, P. ovale and P. cynomolgi can generate latent forms known as hypnozoites (Prudêncio et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prudêncio et al., 2011

claim: Hypnozoites periodically activate several weeks or months after the initial infection to cause malaria relapse.
source: Hypnozoites, triggered by unknown signals, periodically activate several weeks (or even months) after the initial infection to cause malaria relapse (Wells et al., 2010; Shanks and White, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wells et al., 2010 and Shanks and White, 2013

claim: Hypnozoites are triggered by unknown signals.
source: Hypnozoites, triggered by unknown signals, periodically activate several weeks (or even months) after the initial infection to cause malaria relapse (Wells et al., 2010; Shanks and White, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wells et al., 2010 and Shanks and White, 2013

claim: Activation of hypnozoites is responsible for 90% of the global clinical burden associated with relapsing malaria.
source: Activation of hypnozoites was suggested to be responsible for 90% of the global clinical burden associated with relapsing malaria (Adekunle et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adekunle et al., 2015

claim: Recent advances have been made in development of models to study hepatic relapses in vitro.
source: Despite recent advances in development of models to study hepatic relapses in vitro (Dembélé et al., 2014; Gural et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018) and in vivo (Mikolajczak et al., 2015; March et al., 2013), the quest for novel radical cure therapies is stymied by our poor understanding of the molecular determinants of hypnozoite persistence and activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dembélé et al., 2014; Gural et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018

claim: Recent advances have been made in development of models to study hepatic relapses in vivo.
source: Despite recent advances in development of models to study hepatic relapses in vitro (Dembélé et al., 2014; Gural et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018) and in vivo (Mikolajczak et al., 2015; March et al., 2013), the quest for novel radical cure therapies is stymied by our poor understanding of the molecular determinants of hypnozoite persistence and activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mikolajczak et al., 2015; March et al., 2013

claim: The quest for novel radical cure therapies is stymied by poor understanding of the molecular determinants of hypnozoite persistence and activation.
source: Despite recent advances in development of models to study hepatic relapses in vitro (Dembélé et al., 2014; Gural et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2018) and in vivo (Mikolajczak et al., 2015; March et al., 2013), the quest for novel radical cure therapies is stymied by our poor understanding of the molecular determinants of hypnozoite persistence and activation.
evidence: Stated directly in the text

claim: P. cynomolgi is closely related to the P. vivax human malaria parasite.
source: The simian relapsing malaria parasite P. cynomolgi (Pcy)—closely related to the P. vivax human malaria parasite—has been crucial to our current understanding of the hypnozoite biology (Dembélé et al., 2014; Krotoski et al., 1982; Cogswell, 1992; Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017) and the discovery of novel liver-stage active compounds (Zeeman et al., 2014; Zeeman et al., 2016) and anti-relapse drug candidates (Campo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: P. cynomolgi has been crucial to understanding hypnozoite biology.
source: The simian relapsing malaria parasite P. cynomolgi (Pcy)—closely related to the P. vivax human malaria parasite—has been crucial to our current understanding of the hypnozoite biology (Dembélé et al., 2014; Krotoski et al., 1982; Cogswell, 1992; Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017) and the discovery of novel liver-stage active compounds (Zeeman et al., 2014; Zeeman et al., 2016) and anti-relapse drug candidates (Campo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dembélé et al., 2014; Krotoski et al., 1982; Cogswell, 1992; Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017

claim: P. cynomolgi has been crucial to the discovery of novel liver-stage active compounds.
source: The simian relapsing malaria parasite P. cynomolgi (Pcy)—closely related to the P. vivax human malaria parasite—has been crucial to our current understanding of the hypnozoite biology (Dembélé et al., 2014; Krotoski et al., 1982; Cogswell, 1992; Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017) and the discovery of novel liver-stage active compounds (Zeeman et al., 2014; Zeeman et al., 2016) and anti-relapse drug candidates (Campo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zeeman et al., 2014; Zeeman et al., 2016

claim: P. cynomolgi has been crucial to the discovery of anti-relapse drug candidates.
source: The simian relapsing malaria parasite P. cynomolgi (Pcy)—closely related to the P. vivax human malaria parasite—has been crucial to our current understanding of the hypnozoite biology (Dembélé et al., 2014; Krotoski et al., 1982; Cogswell, 1992; Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017) and the discovery of novel liver-stage active compounds (Zeeman et al., 2014; Zeeman et al., 2016) and anti-relapse drug candidates (Campo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campo et al., 2015

claim: LISP2 is a molecular marker of initiation of liver-stage development in relapsing malaria parasites.
source: Here, using in vitro and in vivo liver stage infection models, we demonstrated that LISP2 is a molecular marker of initiation of liver-stage development in relapsing malaria parasites.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments described in the manuscript

claim: The LISP2 marker can assess anti-relapse drug activities in vitro.
source: As proof of concept, using known drugs that have differential effect on hypnozoites, we showed that the LISP2 marker could assess anti-relapse drug activities in vitro.
evidence: Demonstrated through drug experiments described in the manuscript

claim: Comparative transcriptomics analysis of P. cynomolgi liver stages has been carried out.
source: To increase our understanding of the molecular mechanisms that may be underlying the physiological regulation of hypnozoite persistence and activation, we and others have recently carried out comparative transcriptomics analysis of persistent, non-replicating and replicating liver-stages of the P. cynomolgi parasite (Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017; Cubi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017; Cubi et al., 2017

claim: Hypnozoites globally suppress transcription.
source: Searching for potential markers specific to dormancy in our transcriptomic dataset has proven to be difficult because hypnozoites appear to globally suppress transcription and very few genes are specifically up-regulated in hypnozoites (Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017

claim: Very few genes are specifically up-regulated in hypnozoites.
source: Searching for potential markers specific to dormancy in our transcriptomic dataset has proven to be difficult because hypnozoites appear to globally suppress transcription and very few genes are specifically up-regulated in hypnozoites (Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2017

claim: Seven genes were detected above >10 FPKM in hypnozoites and were in the top 5% genes expressed in schizonts.
source: Looking for genes with such an expression pattern, we looked for genes that were detected above >10 FPKM (Fragments Per Kilobase Per Million) in hypnozoite (727 genes) and that were in the top 5% genes expressed in schizonts (134 genes). Amongst the seven genes fulfilling these criteria (most of them were encoding hypothetical proteins; see Supplementary file 1), we identified the gene PcyM_0307500, the P. cynomolgi ortholog of the rodent Plasmodium berghei Liver-Specific Protein 2 (LISP2) (Orito et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on transcriptomic data analysis

claim: PcyM_0307500 is the P. cynomolgi ortholog of P. berghei LISP2.
source: Amongst the seven genes fulfilling these criteria (most of them were encoding hypothetical proteins; see Supplementary file 1), we identified the gene PcyM_0307500, the P. cynomolgi ortholog of the rodent Plasmodium berghei Liver-Specific Protein 2 (LISP2) (Orito et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Orito et al., 2013

claim: In P. cynomolgi, LISP2 is dramatically upregulated (over 72-fold, p-value 0.0009) in replicating schizonts.
source: In P. cynomolgi, LISP2 is dramatically upregulated (over 72-fold, p-value 0.0009) in replicating schizonts but, nonetheless, detectable at significant level (average FPKM 12) in hypnozoites.
evidence: Based on transcriptomic data analysis

claim: LISP2 is detectable at significant level (average FPKM 12) in P. cynomolgi hypnozoites.
source: In P. cynomolgi, LISP2 is dramatically upregulated (over 72-fold, p-value 0.0009) in replicating schizonts but, nonetheless, detectable at significant level (average FPKM 12) in hypnozoites.
evidence: Based on transcriptomic data analysis

claim: A similar expression pattern was reported for P. vivax LISP2 (PVP01_0304700) in the recently published liver stage transcriptome.
source: A similar expression pattern was reported for the P. vivax LISP2 (PVP01_0304700) in the recently published liver stage transcriptome (Gural et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gural et al., 2018

claim: PVP01_0304700 was found to be highly expressed (>150 TPM) in mix population of P. vivax liver stages.
source: PVP01_0304700 was found to be highly expressed in (>150, Transcripts per million, TPM) mix population (mixture of all hepatic stages), whereas it was significantly detected (>25 TPM) in hypnozoite enriched samples above threshold (25 TPM).
evidence: Based on transcriptomic data from Gural et al., 2018

claim: PVP01_0304700 was significantly detected (>25 TPM) in P. vivax hypnozoite enriched samples.
source: PVP01_0304700 was found to be highly expressed in (>150, Transcripts per million, TPM) mix population (mixture of all hepatic stages), whereas it was significantly detected (>25 TPM) in hypnozoite enriched samples above threshold (25 TPM).
evidence: Based on transcriptomic data from Gural et al., 2018

claim: LISP2 protein is 2038 amino-acids long in P. cynomolgi.
source: LISP2 protein is 2038 amino-acids (aa) and 2519 aa long in P. cynomolgi and P. vivax, with an N-terminal signal peptide and a conserved C-terminal 6-cysteine domain (6-cys) found in a family of apicomplexan-specific proteins which are mostly surface proteins (Arredondo and Kappe, 2017; Thompson et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on protein sequence analysis

claim: LISP2 protein is 2519 amino-acids long in P. vivax.
source: LISP2 protein is 2038 amino-acids (aa) and 2519 aa long in P. cynomolgi and P. vivax, with an N-terminal signal peptide and a conserved C-terminal 6-cysteine domain (6-cys) found in a family of apicomplexan-specific proteins which are mostly surface proteins (Arredondo and Kappe, 2017; Thompson et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on protein sequence analysis

claim: LISP2 has an N-terminal signal peptide.
source: LISP2 protein is 2038 amino-acids (aa) and 2519 aa long in P. cynomolgi and P. vivax, with an N-terminal signal peptide and a conserved C-terminal 6-cysteine domain (6-cys) found in a family of apicomplexan-specific proteins which are mostly surface proteins (Arredondo and Kappe, 2017; Thompson et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on protein sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1A

claim: LISP2 has a conserved C-terminal 6-cysteine domain.
source: LISP2 protein is 2038 amino-acids (aa) and 2519 aa long in P. cynomolgi and P. vivax, with an N-terminal signal peptide and a conserved C-terminal 6-cysteine domain (6-cys) found in a family of apicomplexan-specific proteins which are mostly surface proteins (Arredondo and Kappe, 2017; Thompson et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on protein sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The 6-cys domain is found in a family of apicomplexan-specific proteins which are mostly surface proteins.
source: LISP2 protein is 2038 amino-acids (aa) and 2519 aa long in P. cynomolgi and P. vivax, with an N-terminal signal peptide and a conserved C-terminal 6-cysteine domain (6-cys) found in a family of apicomplexan-specific proteins which are mostly surface proteins (Arredondo and Kappe, 2017; Thompson et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arredondo and Kappe, 2017; Thompson et al., 2001

claim: Antibodies were raised against the conserved 6-cys domain for both P. cynomolgi and P. vivax LISP2 proteins.
source: To determine the subcellular localization of LISP2 in relapsing malaria parasites, we raised antibodies against the conserved 6-cys domain for both predicted proteins encoded by the P. cynomolgi (PcyM_0307500) and P. vivax (PVP01_0304700/PVX000975) LISP2 genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The specificity of both P. cynomolgi and P. vivax LISP2 antibodies against the recombinant antigen was confirmed by western blot.
source: We confirmed the specificity of both P. cynomolgi and P. vivax LISP2 antibodies against the recombinant antigen by western blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: LISP2 immunostaining was first observed at day 3 in a characteristic crescent-shape asymmetrically located on one side of early developing liver parasites.
source: LISP2 immunostaining was only observed starting at day 3 in a characteristic crescent-shape asymmetrically located on one side of the early developing liver parasites, or trophozoites (LISP2+).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: By day 4, LISP2 protein is distributed all around the peripheral membrane in a circular pattern around multinucleated parasites.
source: By day 4, LISP2 protein is distributed all around the peripheral membrane in a circular pattern around the parasites that were all very clearly multinucleated (>3 nuclei).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: By day 5, LISP2 accumulates in peripheral vacuolar membrane structures in larger schizonts.
source: By day 5 in larger schizonts, LISP2 appears to accumulate in peripheral vacuolar membrane structures that were not labeled by DAPI or HSP70 antibody (LISP2++).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: LISP2 vacuolar structures were not labeled by DAPI or HSP70 antibody.
source: By day 5 in larger schizonts, LISP2 appears to accumulate in peripheral vacuolar membrane structures that were not labeled by DAPI or HSP70 antibody (LISP2++).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: From day 6 onwards, LISP2 vacuoles were observed as parasites mature and grow to larger schizonts.
source: We observed those vacuoles from day 6 onwards, as the parasites mature and grow to larger schizonts.
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: During the intensive parasite growth phase (Day 4 to Day 10), LISP2 staining was observed in the same vacuolar and peripheral membrane pattern (LISP2++) in multinucleated parasites.
source: During this intensive parasite growth phase (Day 4 to Day 10), LISP2 staining was observed in the same vacuolar and peripheral membrane pattern (LISP2++) in multinucleated parasites (Figure 1B).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: LISP2+ parasites generally appear to have few nuclei.
source: Although the resolution of DAPI staining does not allow for an accurate count of the number of nuclei, LISP2+ parasites generally appear to have few nuclei (see representative images on Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: HSP70 protein is detected during all Plasmodium liver life-cycle stages.
source: The HSP70 protein is detected during all the Plasmodium liver life-cycle stages and HSP70 immunostaining is seen for all parasites from day 1 and throughout the entire 21 days period.
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: The LISP2 transcript is robustly expressed in schizonts but more weakly in a subset of smaller parasites.
source: We independently confirmed this expression pattern at the RNA level in Fluorescent In Situ Hybridization (FISH) experiments in P. cynomolgi cultures. Indeed, the LISP2 transcript is robustly expressed in schizonts but more weakly in a subset of smaller parasites (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by FISH experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: LISP2 expression is first observed at day 3 post-infection in P. vivax with an identical crescent staining located at one side of the membrane.
source: Similar to the in vitro observations with P. cynomolgi parasites, LISP2 expression is first observed at days 3 post-infection in P. vivax with an identical crescent staining located at one side of the membrane.
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments in huHep mice shown in Figure 2A

claim: A large fraction of non-replicating small parasites (hypnozoites) were devoid of LISP2 expression in P. vivax from day 3 to day 18.
source: During the course of development from day 3 to day 18, we observed a large fraction of non-replicating small parasites (hypnozoites) that were devoid of LISP2 expression in P. vivax.
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments in huHep mice shown in Figure 2A

claim: At each time point (days 3, 5, 8 and 18), LISP2- hypnozoites and LISP2+ trophozoites were of similar size ranges in P. vivax.
source: At each time point (days 3, 5, 8 and 18), LISP2- hypnozoite and LISP2+ trophozoite were of similar size ranges.
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments in huHep mice shown in Figure 2A

claim: UIS4 protein accumulated in a characteristic prominence in established mature P. vivax hypnozoites.
source: As reported earlier, UIS4 protein accumulated in a characteristic prominence in established mature hypnozoites (Mikolajczak et al., 2015) as well as in LISP2+ trophozoites while in mature schizonts the entire parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) were stained (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 2A and supported by citation to Mikolajczak et al., 2015

claim: UIS4 protein accumulated in LISP2+ trophozoites.
source: As reported earlier, UIS4 protein accumulated in a characteristic prominence in established mature hypnozoites (Mikolajczak et al., 2015) as well as in LISP2+ trophozoites while in mature schizonts the entire parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) were stained (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: In mature schizonts, the entire parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) was stained by UIS4.
source: As reported earlier, UIS4 protein accumulated in a characteristic prominence in established mature hypnozoites (Mikolajczak et al., 2015) as well as in LISP2+ trophozoites while in mature schizonts the entire parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) were stained (Figure 2A).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: UIS4 and LISP2 proteins co-localized at the PVM prominence in LISP2+ trophozoites at all time-points.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that UIS4 and LISP2 proteins co-localized at the PVM prominence in LISP2+ trophozoites at all time-points (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed in IFA experiments shown in Figure 2B

claim: P. cynomolgi hypnozoites exhibit the UIS4-prominence.
source: We could not perform UIS4 and LISP2 co-staining in P. cynomolgi as both antibodies were made in same species, notwithstanding we could demonstrate the presence of UIS4 PVM prominence in established hypnozoites in P. cynomolgi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in IFA experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: LISP2 is expressed in early developing liver stage parasites and represents a marker for initiation of liver stage schizogony in relapsing malaria species.
source: Collectively, the above data from in vitro and in vivo suggests that LISP2 is expressed in early developing liver stage parasites and represents a marker for initiation of liver stage schizogony in relapsing malaria species.
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo data

claim: At day 6 post-infection, 23% of P. cynomolgi liver stage parasites robustly expressed LISP2 protein (LISP2++).
source: In total, 23% of the day 6 liver stage parasites robustly expressed the LISP2 protein (LISP2++), whereas the vast majority of the liver stage parasites (73%) remained smaller, uni-nucleated, and did not react with the LISP2 monoclonal antibodies (LISP2-).
evidence: Quantified from IFA experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: At day 6 post-infection, 73% of P. cynomolgi liver stage parasites remained smaller, uni-nucleated, and did not react with LISP2 antibodies (LISP2-).
source: In total, 23% of the day 6 liver stage parasites robustly expressed the LISP2 protein (LISP2++), whereas the vast majority of the liver stage parasites (73%) remained smaller, uni-nucleated, and did not react with the LISP2 monoclonal antibodies (LISP2-).
evidence: Quantified from IFA experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: At day 6 post-infection, 4% of P. cynomolgi parasites were LISP2 positive trophozoites with a characteristic crescent-shape LISP2 staining pattern (LISP2+).
source: In addition to these large multinucleated parasites, we also observed a small fraction of LISP2 positive trophozoites (4%) with a characteristic crescent-shape LISP2 staining pattern (LISP2+) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Quantified from IFA experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: Persistent LISP2- hypnozoites increase in size from about 1 μm diameter to reach a plateau at about 6 μm diameter by day 8-9.
source: In the first 8–9 days, persistent LISP2- hypnozoites increase in size from about 1 μm diameter to reach a plateau at about 6 μm diameter on average.
evidence: Measured from growth kinetics shown in Figure 3B

claim: Persistent P. vivax hypnozoites undergo a slight growth phase in vivo.
source: Similarly, persistent P. vivax hypnozoites have been reported to undergo a slight growth phase in vivo (Mikolajczak et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mikolajczak et al., 2015

claim: The size of LISP2+ trophozoites does not change over time and remained constant from day 3 to day 21 at a median size of 6.9 μm in diameter.
source: In sharp contrast, the size of LISP2+ trophozoites does not change over time and remained constant from day 3 to day 21 at a median size of 6.9 μm (5th to 95th percentile; 6.3 and 7.3) in diameter (Figure 3B).
evidence: Measured from growth kinetics shown in Figure 3B

claim: From day 7 to day 8 onwards, LISP2- hypnozoites and LISP2+ trophozoites were indistinguishable by size.
source: Thus, remarkably, from day 7 to day 8 onwards, LISP2- hypnozoites and LISP2+ trophozoites were indistinguishable by size.
evidence: Inferred from growth kinetics data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Developing LISP2++ liver stage schizonts were significantly bigger at day 4 with a median diameter of 9.4 μm.
source: As expected, developing LISP2++ liver stage schizonts were significantly bigger at day 4 with a median diameter of 9.4 μm (5th to 95th percentile; 6.9 and 15.1) and continue to grow to reach a plateau by day 10 with a median size of about 21.6 μm (5th to 95th percentile; 9.1 and 49) in diameter for mature schizonts.
evidence: Measured from growth kinetics shown in Figure 3B

claim: LISP2++ schizonts continue to grow to reach a plateau by day 10 with a median size of about 21.6 μm in diameter.
source: As expected, developing LISP2++ liver stage schizonts were significantly bigger at day 4 with a median diameter of 9.4 μm (5th to 95th percentile; 6.9 and 15.1) and continue to grow to reach a plateau by day 10 with a median size of about 21.6 μm (5th to 95th percentile; 9.1 and 49) in diameter for mature schizonts.
evidence: Measured from growth kinetics shown in Figure 3B

claim: LISP2+ parasites may be appearing continuously throughout the culture period and develop into LISP2++ maturing schizonts.
source: Collectively, the LISP2 expression pattern suggested that LISP2+ parasites may be appearing continuously throughout the culture period and develop into LISP2++ maturing schizonts ranging from 7 to 8 µm up to 49 µm in diameter.
